items.stimulus: Forecasters have long relied on a simple rule for lake-effect snow: heavy bands form only when the air passing over a lake is at least 13°C colder than the water's surface. Meteorologist Lena Okafor, however, argues that this rule leaves out wind direction. When wind blows along a lake's full length, the air gathers heat and moisture over a much longer stretch of water. Okafor's records show that such winds have produced heavy snow even when the temperature gap was only 8°C.
items.stem: Based on the text, Okafor would most likely agree with which statement about lake-effect snow?
choices: Heavy lake-effect snow forms only when the air is at least 13°C colder than the lake.
Heavy snow can form with a small temperature gap if wind crosses the lake's full length.
The temperature gap between air and water has no effect on whether snow bands form.
Wind direction matters less to lake-effect snow than forecasters have usually assumed.
items.explanation: After 'however,' the passage gives Okafor's claim: wind blowing along a lake's full length can produce heavy snow even with an 8°C gap, well under the 13°C rule. Choice B applies that claim directly.

A.why: This is the forecasters' rule that Okafor is arguing against. You picked the view the passage explains first instead of the one that comes after 'however.'

C.why: Okafor says the rule is incomplete, not that temperature doesn't matter. You took her point further than she does.

D.why: This reverses Okafor's view. She argues that wind direction matters more than the traditional rule allows.

Conifers appeared in the fossil record later than flowering plants did.

items.stimulus: In principle, linguists separate languages from dialects with one test: if speakers of two varieties can understand each other, they speak dialects of a single language. items.stem: Based on the text, Moreau would most likely agree with which statement about the line between languages and dialects?

How varieties are labeled often reflects politics as well as whether speakers understand each other.
Speech varieties are so alike that they cannot be meaningfully grouped or classified at all.
Political boundaries have little influence on how speech varieties come to be labeled.
items.explanation: Moreau says the line is 'often drawn by politics' and is 'less purely linguistic than it seems.' That means labels reflect politics as well as whether speakers understand each other, which is what B says.

items.stimulus: When public health agencies tally the deaths caused by a heat wave, they have traditionally counted the death certificates that list heatstroke as the cause. Epidemiologist Rana Okafor, however, argues that this method captures only a small share of the toll. Extreme heat, she notes, most often kills by straining the hearts and kidneys of people who are already ill, and such deaths are usually certified as cardiac or renal failure. Okafor contends that a more accurate count comes from comparing all deaths during a heat wave with the number normally expected for that time of year.
items.stem: Based on the text, Okafor would most likely agree with which statement about a city that recorded four heatstroke deaths during a recent heat wave?
choices: The figure of four is a dependable measure of the toll, since a physician certified the cause of each of those deaths.
The heat wave's true toll may be much higher, which comparing total deaths with the usual number for that week could reveal.
The city's death certificates are too unreliable to be used in studying any cause of death, including heart and kidney failure.
The heat wave's true toll is probably higher, because many people with heatstroke die at home without ever reaching a hospital.
items.explanation: Okafor's claim is that heat deaths are mostly recorded under other causes, so heatstroke certificates undercount them, and that comparing total deaths with the expected number gives a better figure. Applied to this city, four heatstroke deaths could hide a much larger toll, and her proposed comparison is the way to find it.

Flowering plants probably arose later than the oldest known fossil flowers suggest.

items.subtype_name: What a named researcher or critic would most likely believe or agree with
items.stimulus: Engineers have long traced metal fatigue to the surface: a scratch concentrates stress, a crack begins there, and polishing is the routine remedy. Materials scientist Ines Valdivia argues that this account fits poorly with 3D-printed aluminum parts. In her tests, most fatigue cracks in printed brackets began at tiny gas pores sealed inside the metal during printing, well beneath the surface. Polishing those brackets, she found, extended their service life only slightly.
items.stem: Based on the text, Valdivia would most likely agree with all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Reducing pores formed during printing would likely lengthen a printed bracket's life more than polishing it would.
Surface scratches can still concentrate some stress in a printed aluminum bracket, even if they are not the main problem.
Polishing is the most effective way to delay fatigue cracking in a printed aluminum bracket.
Inspecting only the surface of a printed bracket may miss the flaws most likely to make it fail.
items.explanation: Valdivia's claim is that in printed aluminum, most cracks start at internal pores, so polishing helps 'only slightly.' Calling polishing the most effective remedy is the conventional surface account she argues against. She would reject it, so it is the exception.

A.why: The text never mentions reducing pores, so this may have looked like it claimed too much. But if pores cause most cracks and polishing barely helps, you can infer that fewer pores would help more. That is her argument applied to a new case, which is exactly what this question asks you to do.

B.why: This mentions surface scratches, so you may have taken it for the view Valdivia rejects. Read it to the end. It only says scratches matter a little, and her finding that polishing helped 'slightly' supports that. She narrows the surface account. She doesn't throw it out.

D.why: Inspection isn't mentioned in the text, so this may have looked unsupported. But the cracks begin 'well beneath the surface,' so checking only the surface would miss them. It follows directly from her finding.

items.stimulus: Firms worried about turnover usually reach for the obvious tool: higher wages, on the assumption that workers quit mainly to earn more elsewhere. Economist Priya Raman contends that for hourly warehouse staff, this assumption misses the main cause. A warehouse with high turnover might gain more from posting shifts early than from a modest raise.
Firms that rely on raises alone to reduce turnover may be using the wrong tool.
How far ahead shifts are posted can affect whether hourly workers stay.
items.explanation: Raman argues that the usual assumption, that workers quit mainly for pay, 'misses the main cause' for warehouse staff. Choice A restates the very view she rejects, so it is the one she would not agree with.

B.why: The text doesn't advise any particular warehouse, so this may have seemed to go too far. But early posting cut quits by nearly a third and a modest raise did almost nothing. Applying that finding to a warehouse with high turnover is the extension her argument supports.

C.why: You may have seen 'raises' at the start and matched it to the view about wages. Read the whole choice. It says relying on raises alone may be the wrong tool, which agrees with Raman.

D.why: This may have looked like a detail from her data rather than her opinion. Still, it is a statement she would accept, because her whole finding rests on it. In a NOT question, a true statement is never the answer.

items.subtype_name: What a named researcher or critic would most likely believe or agree with
items.stimulus: Paleobotanists have traditionally sorted Carboniferous fern-like fossils into two groups: true ferns, which spread by spores, and seed ferns, which bore seeds. Leaf shape was long treated as a reliable guide to which group a fossil belonged to. Paleobotanist Hana Lindqvist challenges that reliance. Examining 300 specimens with preserved reproductive structures, she found nearly identical fronds in both groups, suggesting that leaf shape alone cannot reveal how a plant reproduced.
items.stem: Based on the text, Lindqvist would most likely agree with all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Fronds of very similar shape could belong to plants that reproduced in different ways.
Spore-bearing and seed-bearing plants of the period really did differ in how they reproduced.
Some fossils assigned to a group on the basis of leaves alone may need to be reexamined.
The difference between true ferns and seed ferns is too slight to be worth recording.
items.explanation: Lindqvist questions one sorting method, using leaf shape. She does not question the two groups themselves, which she identified by their reproductive structures. Saying the difference isn't worth recording pushes her claim much further than she takes it, so she would reject it.

A.why: This may have looked like a restatement of her evidence rather than her belief. But it is her finding, and she would plainly agree with it. Finding a true statement isn't enough in a NOT question. You need the one that fails.

B.why: This sounds like the traditional view, so you may have assumed she rejects it. She doesn't. She relies on the spore and seed difference to sort her own specimens. What she rejects is leaf shape as a guide to that difference.

C.why: The text doesn't mention reexamining older fossils, so this may have looked like overreach. But if leaf shape can't reveal how a plant reproduced, then assignments based only on leaves are open to doubt. That follows from her claim.
